## You!

* Turn to your neighbor and introduce yourself 👋  
* Together, come up with **one binary question** that you think will divide the class **about in half**  

* Examples:  
  * Coke or Pepsi?  
  * Spaghetti or Sushi?  
  * Morning person or Night owl?  

## Let's Play a Game

**Rules:**

* Everyone starts with their hand up
* Each turn, a student poses a _valid_ yes/no question  
  + **YES** = Put your hand down
  + **NO** = Keep it up
* **YES** people are now on vacation 🌴 (your hand stays down from now on — relax and enjoy!)  

* A question is _valid_ if more than four and less than half the remaining people say "yes"

**End of Game:**

* We stop when **ten or fewer people** remain in play
* Everyone else is happily **on vacation** 🌴  

::: notes

How to Count

Start w 150 (say)
pose question 1, 5 <= k1 <= 150/2 down -> 150-k1 remain. 
pose 2, 5 <= k2 down <= (150-k1)/2 -> 150-k1-k2 remain. 
pose question 3, 5 <= k3 <= (150-k1-k2)/2 -> 150-k1-k2-k3 remain. etc. 

:::

## Debrief 💡

Punchline questions:  

* What is the minimum number of questions?

* What is the maximum number of questions?

*  Why did we stop at 10 instead of 1?

* Why did we do this game?


::: notes

- Best case: keep halving ⇒ about **log₂(150/10) ≈ 4 rounds**  
- Worst case: only 5 eliminated each round ⇒ ~28 rounds  
- Stopping at 10 = “small enough to brute force”  
  → common strategy in algorithms  

:::

## About This Course

This course will teach you a bunch of different things!

- (More) Python!
- New data types and patterns: classes, dictionaries, tables, graphs
- Data science: pandas, data frames, visualizations
- Algorithms and complexity
- Art and creativity: lots of examples!
- Tools and Techniques(?): Terminal, marimo, PrairieLearn, unit tests, Markdown, Git,

## Course Components: Lecture and Take-Home

All elements are accessed through [PrairieLearn]({{< var course.prairielearn >}}).

- Lectures: Tuesdays and Thursdays, in-class activities based on problem solving and design.
- Labs: Mondays / Tuesdays / Thursdays, practice on lecture material.
  * Released on Sunday night, due the following Sunday night.
- Problems of the week (POTW): One per (week)day, ~ 50 / term.
  * Released in batches of five on Sunday night, due the following Sunday night.
- Projects: Three total, involve more substantial programming practice.
  * Released on Monday morning, due three weeks later.

## Course Components 2: Invigilated {.smaller}

- Examlets: Five, roughly every two weeks.
  * Schedule your own 50 minute block.
  * Available Thursday through Monday.
- Final Exam:
  * Schedule your own 110(?) minute block.
  * Available during a five day window TBA.
  * Practice version released a week before.
* You will physically go to an [ORCA](https://orca.ubc.ca/students/) facility.
* Scheduling is done through [PrairieTest]({{< var course.prairietest >}}).
  * Opens Tuesday at 10:00am, two weeks before the assessment.
* Practice versions released through [PrairieLearn]({{< var course.prairielearn >}}) a week before.

# How to Succeed in CPSC 203

## On the use of computers in class

Laptop use is encouraged in CPSC 203 lectures and labs 

However, there is a restriction:

- You may **only** use your laptop (or other screens, such as phones) for CPSC 203 material. 
  * Using screens for other purposes has been shown to reduce your learning and **lower your grades**.
  * Using screens for other purposes has also been shown to **reduce the grades of those around you**.
- If you have something urgent to do, just leave the classroom!

## How to Study

- This is **learn by doing** material!
  - Passively watching videos / live coding and reading our solutions will not be enough.
  - You must solve the problems yourself and write out their solutions.
- There are many opportunities for you to practice:
  - In lecture, labs, POTWs, practice examlets, projects, ...

## From a Former CPSC 110 Student (Applies to CPSC 203 too)

> It's funny how repetition in actually doing the work leads to it all of a sudden making sense to me. I can't explain it. I don't have a sense of growing understanding. I have confusion, repetition, and suddenly a sense of understanding. It's not coming through watching or reading, though. It comes from replicating what I've watched several times. This has happened repeatedly for me in this class. I start the week with a sense of accomplishment, well being, peace of mind, and confidence from the victory over last week's homework. I am then submerged in doubt, confusion, and erm, terror. (Why not be melodramatic?) Suddenly there is a working epiphany and I have victory again.

## Possible sources of negative emotions

- Feeling confused about a topic.
- Feeling of falling behind/not having enough time.
- Some external event.
- Something else.

**We can usually find a solution!**

- Talk to us!
